claim: CloudFront recommends origin access control (OAC) instead of origin access identity (OAI) for sending authenticated requests to an Amazon S3 origin; OAC was added on 2022-08-24.
question: Which does CloudFront recommend for restricting an S3 origin to CloudFront: origin access identity (OAI) or origin access control (OAC)?

values.display: use OAC instead
origin access identity (OAI)

qualifiers.scope: CloudFront with an Amazon S3 origin
qualifiers.condition: OAI still works and is the older mechanism

evidence.quote: We recommend that you use OAC instead because it supports the following features:
CloudFront provides two ways to send authenticated requests to an Amazon S3 origin: origin access control (OAC) and origin access identity (OAI).

| [Enhanced security with origin access control](private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.md) | You can now secure Amazon S3 origins by permitting access to only the designated CloudFront distributions. | August 24, 2022 |

note: d127, d140. Current-truth fact for the OAC change. Older practice questions say 'use an OAI'; the best answer is now OAC. Change fact: cloudfront-change-oac-s3-origins-2022-08.

claim: To restrict content to selected users, for example users who have paid a fee, you serve it through CloudFront with signed URLs or signed cookies.
question: Which CloudFront control fits 'only paid subscribers can view the content'?

values.display: users who have paid a fee
using signed URLs or signed cookies

evidence.quote: You can restrict access to content that is intended for selected users—for example, users who have paid a fee—by serving this private content through CloudFront using signed URLs or signed cookies.

claim: Lambda@Edge functions run in a regional edge cache, usually in the AWS Region closest to the CloudFront edge location that the client reached.
question: Where does Lambda@Edge code run compared with CloudFront Functions?

values.display: executed in a regional edge cache
the AWS region closest to the CloudFront edge location

evidence.quote: Lambda@Edge functions are executed in a regional edge cache (usually in the AWS region closest to the CloudFront edge location reached by the client).
Once associated to a CloudFront distribution, the code is deployed to AWS’s globally distributed network of edge locations for execution in response to CloudFront requests.

note: d139. The first quote is about Lambda@Edge; the second, from the CloudFront Functions FAQ answer, says CloudFront Functions code is deployed to the edge locations.

claim: For a global audience you can create an accelerator to get global static addresses announced from AWS edge locations around the world, while an Elastic IP address is a static IPv4 address associated with an EC2 instance or network interface in a single Region.
question: When do you choose Global Accelerator static IP addresses instead of an Elastic IP address?

values.display: global static addresses that are announced from AWS edge locations around the world
in a single AWS Region

qualifiers.scope: AWS Global Accelerator compared with Elastic IP addresses

evidence.quote: If you have a global audience, you can create an accelerator with Global Accelerator to get global static addresses that are announced from AWS edge locations around the world.
For example, you can allocate an Elastic IP address, which is a static IPv4 address that you can associate with an Amazon EC2 instance or network interface in a single AWS Region.

note: d121, d137. Docs page version of the FAQ comparison.

claim: Global Accelerator creates a peering connection with your VPC using private IP addresses, which keeps connections to internal Application Load Balancers or private EC2 instances off the public internet; you use private subnets to ensure traffic is delivered only by Global Accelerator.
question: How does Global Accelerator reach internal load balancers and private EC2 instances?

values.display: creates a peering connection with your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud using private IP addresses
Use private subnets to ensure that traffic is delivered only by Global Accelerator

qualifiers.scope: AWS Global Accelerator endpoints in a VPC
qualifiers.condition: the VPC has an internet gateway attached; public IP addresses and an internet gateway route are not needed

evidence.quote: Global Accelerator creates a peering connection with your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud using private IP addresses, keeping connections to your internal Application Load Balancers or private EC2 instances off the public internet.
Use private subnets to ensure that traffic is delivered only by Global Accelerator.
